prs.title: feat(protocol): carry attachment bytes inside a group
prs.body:
**Stacked on #449, which is stacked on #448.** Base is
`feat/data-layer-f7-interest`; review and merge in order.

An attachment reference replicated to every member of a group and the bytes
reached nobody. Fetching them needed a confirmed pairwise session, and two
members of a group need not have one with each other, so a reference in a
group was a hash the application could see and never resolve. This is the
last of the bullets under "What this version does not do" that this series
set out to close.

## What this adds

`fetchAttachmentFrom(space, peer, hash)` asks one member of a group for the
bytes, and they come back as `chunk` frames sealed under the group key, which
is membership and needs no handshake. `provideAttachment` and
`declineAttachment` now accept a group space, with the member that asked as
the peer.

## Why the fetch names a member

Two reasons, and the second is the one that is easy to miss.

A reference says what the bytes are and nothing about who holds them, so
somebody has to choose. The SDK does not try members in turn, because each
miss costs the whole silence timeout and a reference nobody holds would spend
one per member; the application knows who wrote the reference.

And a directed frame is **promoted to a roster-wide delivery** when the
sender's ratchet budget runs out, which means a request arrives at every
member whether or not it was addressed to them, and a receiver cannot tell
the two apart. Without the addressee in the frame, every member's application
is asked for bytes the requester can accept from only one of them. `need_blob`
therefore carries `to` inside a group.

That one is a defect this PR fixes rather than a design note: it was found
because a test assertion encoded the intent ("a directed request reached a
member it was not addressed to") and failed.

## The size cap, and why it is not a window

A group attachment is at most 32 frames of 32 KiB, 1 MiB in all. That bound
is what keeps `need_blob` a single-hop question: the whole answer leaves at
once, so nothing has to ask for the next window and there is no chain of
questions to terminate. "Every leg ends" is not weakened at all.

The plan for this stage had a windowed protocol with a `need_chunks` frame, a
holder keeping bytes between windows, and a re-ask clock. That is the
machinery the media path already has, and growing a second copy of it on the
frame path was the largest and riskiest part of the work. The cap buys it
out. `provideAttachment` refuses a larger blob at the call, while the
application still has the file in hand, and says to use a 1:1 session
instead. Nothing about the 1:1 path changed.

## What admits a chunk

Only an outstanding request, and only from the member that request was put
to. The first bounds what a member can spend of another's memory, and
promotion guarantees such chunks arrive at members who asked for nothing; the
second stops one member answering, or refusing, a question put to somebody
else. Neither substitutes for checking that the assembled bytes hash to the
address that was asked for, which is the only check that says what the bytes
*are*.

## What deliberately did not change

Documents too large for a frame are still 1:1. A blob is *asked for*, so a
chunk of one is admitted against a request; a carried document is unsolicited
by design, so frames carrying one would be admitted on nothing but the
sender's say-so, and a member could spend every other member's memory by
sending them. A group version needs a rule this layer does not have. The spec
says so, so nobody finishes the job by symmetry.

## Compatibility

Negotiated as `data_versions` entry 6, appended, and the first entry since
the second to have an attested sibling: a group inviter now attests every
group-relevant entry it knows about a member rather than only entry 2. A
member without entry 6 refuses the request whose shape it knows and drops the
chunk frames whose kind it does not, so nothing is shown to anybody wrongly;
what the entry buys is refusing a fetch at the call instead of leaving an
application waiting out the timeout.

`pending_attachment_fetches` is now gated on the `data` feature, because its
value type is. The `--no-default-features` clippy job caught that.

## Verification

A spike ran before any of this was built, and both halves are now regression
tests: 64 directed frames all decrypt in one epoch and reach nobody else, and
a run survives the ratchet promotion with the promoted frame reaching every
other member exactly once.

Eight mechanisms mutation-checked. Three came back uncaught on the first run.
One was a bad mutation of mine that changed nothing, which is its own lesson.
The other two were real gaps with no test at all — the chunk-shape bound and
a refusal from the wrong member — and both now have tests that assert the
carriage *survives* the malformed input rather than only that it was ignored.

Green locally: `cargo fmt`, both clippy jobs, `cargo test --workspace` (2,933
passed), rustdoc, regenerated bindings, the uniffi drift guards, the Android
JVM suite, `tsc --noEmit`, and the Python suite against a real cdylib.



---

**CI note.** This repository runs CI only on pull requests targeting `main`
(`.github/workflows/ci.yml`), so the checks above are the contributor licence
check alone while this PR is stacked. GitHub retargets it to `main` when its
base merges, and the full matrix runs then.

The combined state is verified locally in the meantime: the tip of
`feat/data-layer-f8-group-blobs` contains all three stages, and the full gate
loop passes on it — `cargo fmt`, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`,
`clippy -p offline-protocol --no-default-features`, `cargo test --workspace`
(2,933 passed, 0 failed), `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, regenerated
bindings, the uniffi drift guards, the Android JVM suite, `tsc --noEmit`, and
the Python suite against a real cdylib.

---

## Review pass (rebased onto `main`, six commits on top)

The stack below this has merged, so the branch is rebased onto `main` and
the checks now run against the real base. Six commits answer the review.

**A group fetch that ends now names the member it was put to.**
`data_attachment_unavailable` carried `peer_id: space`, which is the peer on
a 1:1 space and the *group id* in a group, so every road but `declined`
reported the group where the event's own documentation promises the member
asked. Forgetting a peer also missed group questions put to them, because it
matched on the key prefix and the key composes the space.

**A request goes only to a member known to receive it.** This is the one
directed frame that is a question rather than an answer, so nothing the
member already sent stands as proof they intercept `__DATA_V1__`, and it was
gated on roster membership alone: a member on a build that does not
intercept them was handed the question as chat text. It now answers to the
same per-member predicate the roster-wide gate is built from, which matters
because a directed frame can be promoted into a roster-wide delivery. The
inviter's attestation is what supplies that knowledge for members never
dealt with directly, which is the ordinary case and is why entry 6 has an
attested sibling.

**The entry-6 refusal never fired.** It read direct knowledge as membership
of entry 1's set alone, so a peer known only by a later entry looked like
one never heard from. The earlier suite passed with that gate stubbed out to
always allow; it now has tests, as does the attestation road.

**Falling back to a second member works.** The repeat window was keyed by
space and blob, neither of which changes when the member does, so a fallback
inside the window returned `Ok` and asked nobody, and after it discarded
whatever the first member had sent. A different member is now a new
question and the displaced one is reported by name. A fetch naming this
device is refused rather than waiting out the timeout.

**Chunks are kept to the road that carries them.** A chunk was admitted on a
1:1 session too, where the media path already answers a fetch with its own
reassembly, caps and failure report.

Plus: the assembly's unread byte counter is gone and its bound stated
structurally, the spec carries the three new rules, the bounds table and
threat model name what one member can hold of another's memory, and the
three stale "blob carriage is 1:1" claims and three em dashes are fixed.

Mutation-checked: the entry-6 gate mutation that survived before now fails,
as do the entry-2 gate, the `peer_id` fix, the 1:1 chunk guard and the
per-chunk size bound. Green locally on the rebased tree: `cargo fmt`, both
clippy jobs, `cargo test --workspace`, rustdoc under `-D warnings`. No UDL
or uniffi change, so the bindings are untouched.

prs.title: feat(protocol): replicate part of a space, by document name
prs.body:
**No longer stacked.** #448 is merged, and this is rebased onto `main` as a
single commit plus its review fixes. Base is `main`; it merges on its own.

A space replicated whole or not at all, so a device that wanted one document
out of a thousand paid for the thousand: storage for what it never reads, and
radio for every one of them on every exchange. This is the second of the
three bullets under "What this version does not do".

## What this adds

`setInterest(space, patterns)` names the documents this device wants from its
peers. Each pattern is a document name, optionally ending in `*` to match a
prefix; `["*"]` is everything and is the default, `[]` is nothing, and a
space takes at most 32. A space nobody narrows behaves exactly as before and
its frames are byte-identical to the ones it sends today.

## Two halves that fail differently

**Toward a peer it is a request.** Every version offer carries it, so the
peer answers only with what was asked for. That is the bandwidth saving, and
it needs the peer to read the field.

**Here it is a refusal.** A document outside the patterns is never created
from an offer and never imported however it arrives. That half depends on
nothing, which is why a narrowed space is narrow even against a peer that
ignores the request, including every build that predates it.

## Three rules that keep it from losing documents

1. **The answer is scoped by the asker's declared interest, never by the
   names their frame happened to carry.** The second is how a document the
   peer has never seen gets dropped with no symptom on either device; this
   repository has paid for that shape once already, and the MUST NOT against
   it is untouched.
2. **A counter-offer carries the complete list.** Scoping it would save one
   name per unwanted document and buy back the hazard in rule 1. The saving
   worth having is the *document*, which the catch-up loop already declines
   to send.
3. **Removals are never scoped.** A peer that narrows keeps what it already
   held, so a removal for a document it no longer wants is exactly the one it
   still needs.

## Behaviour worth knowing

Interest is **not persisted**: it is application policy for a launch rather
than a fact about the store, and a durable copy would be a second thing to
reconcile against an app that changed its mind. Declare it before `start()`.

**Narrowing does not delete what is already held**, because a policy change
should not destroy data nobody asked to lose; those documents stop being
updated and stay where they are. **Widening asks**, since the newly wanted
documents are absent from this device's next offer and inside its declared
interest.

## Compatibility

Negotiated as `data_versions` entry 5, appended. On the wire an absent `want`
means everything and an empty one means nothing, and the two are deliberately
not collapsed: collapsing them would turn the narrowest request a sender can
make into the widest. No storage change, no config change, no new error code.

## Verification

Eight mechanisms mutation-checked, each failing only for its own mutation.
One came back uncaught and was the recurring vacuous-gate shape: the test for
the per-frame pattern bound asserted only that an answer came back, which is
true whether or not the bound exists. It now puts the matching pattern
*past* the bound and counts frames, so it asserts both halves — the offer is
still answered, and the patterns beyond the bound are not honoured.

Green locally: `cargo fmt`, both clippy jobs, `cargo test --workspace` (2,923
passed), rustdoc, regenerated bindings, the uniffi drift guards, the Android
JVM suite, `tsc --noEmit`, and the Python suite against a real cdylib.

## Note for the reviewer

`send_version_frames` and `answer_version_offer` grew past clippy's argument
limit, so the three fields an offer carries (`docs`, `gone`, `want`) are now
an `OfferContents` struct. They travel together in both directions and two of
them have the same type, so passing them separately was three arguments a
caller could transpose.



---

## Review fixes

Reviewed, then rebased onto `main`. The rebase mattered: the earlier green
matrix ran while #448 was still open, so it tested this work on the
pre-review F6 and never on the merged one. Two conflicts came out of that
overlap, and one of them is load-bearing: #448 moved the removal-floor check
into `apply_contained_blob` behind an in-flight marker because it is an
engine decode of a peer's bytes, so the interest refusal now sits *above*
it. Placed below, a narrowed space would pay that decode for documents it
then drops.

Eight fixes on top:

- `data_set_interest` now goes through `require_data_storage()`. It was the
  only `DataStore` method that returned `Ok` with the layer off, which an
  application would read as a narrowing it never got.
- `validate_interest_pattern` strips the trailing `*` and delegates to
  `validate_name` instead of carrying a second copy of the document charset.
- The entry-5 wire gate is now actually asserted. Its test checked only that
  the unwanted document went unstored, which is true whether or not the
  request was suppressed; it counts frames now, where the gate is the
  difference between two and three.
- New group-channel test. Interest is declared unconditionally there, so the
  local refusal is the only thing carrying a narrowing on that channel, and
  nothing covered it.
- The `want` field is noted against the version-frame budget, so nobody has
  to re-derive that 32 patterns of 128 bytes fits inside it.
- The upgrade guide entry is numbered §23 and no longer re-introduces the
  pre-rename `data_doc_deleted`.
- Spec rule 2 said `MAY NOT`, which RFC 2119 does not define. Now `MUST NOT`.
- Two em dashes, and a stray changelog blank line.

**CI.** All 19 checks pass on the rebased head, which is the first run
against the real combination. `Test (ubuntu-latest)` failed once on
`everyone_hearing_everyone_does_not_multiply_the_traffic`, a mesh-gossip
test with no reference to the document layer that passed on macOS, Windows
and locally; it passed on re-run.

Also green locally: `cargo fmt`, both clippy jobs, `cargo test --workspace`,
rustdoc under `-D warnings`, `generate-bindings.sh` (a clean no-op, so the
committed bindings are the ones this UDL produces), the Python suite against
a real cdylib, and `tsc --noEmit`.


---

## Second review pass

Reviewed again on the rebased head, where CI had finally run against the
merged F6 rather than the pre-review one. The design held; six things did
not. One commit each.

**`wipeAll` left the interest behind.** It clears the documents, the space
index, the removal records, every offer window and every outstanding fetch,
and its own doc comment promises that nothing distinguishes a wiped space
from one this device has never seen. A surviving narrowing is exactly such a
distinction, and because `wipeAll` is the logout path it was one account's
policy silently applied to the next account that replicates with the same
peer.

**A `setInterest` before `start()` spent the offer window.** That is the
documented order, and there the frame cannot leave the device: the
transports are not up, so it is dropped for want of a session. The offer path
has stamped the 30 second window by then, and that stamp went on to suppress
the sweep `start()` makes and the first rediscovery after it. Peer
capabilities are restored in `initialize_mls`, so the gate that would have
stopped it is already open. Declaring the same patterns at every launch, which
is what a fixed policy does, spent the same window on an offer identical to
the last one. Neither case loses a question: the start-up sweep and every
rediscovery build their offer from the interest as it stands.

**A carried snapshot outside the interest was reassembled first.** The media
road reached the refusal only at the import, after up to the record ceiling
of bytes had been buffered to reach a decision the application already made.
The document name is in the descriptor, where the size ceiling is judged for
exactly the same reason, so the refusal moved there. Only a peer without
entry 5 sends one, so nothing regresses.

**The two bounds were two unlinked 32s.** `MAX_INTEREST_PATTERNS` bounds what
an application may set, `MAX_INTEREST_PATTERNS_PER_FRAME` what a receiver
reads. Raising the first alone would have every peer drop the tail of every
list with no symptom on either device. A const assert now fails at the edit.

**Three things the spec left to be re-derived.** The answer table still said a
`reply: true` offer draws a catch-up for each stale document, when both legs
scope by the declared want. The pattern bound was required but never given a
number, while every other limit under Sizes is stated. And interest does not
narrow what a removal costs: a floor is recorded for a removed name whether or
not the declarer wants it, because a floor refused on interest is one a
widening has to re-acquire, and until the next offer carries it again a third
replica offering the removed content would have it created here. That is the
removal undone by the replica that outlived it, which is what floors exist to
prevent, so a narrowed space spends the same per-space ceiling as a whole one.
Said in the spec and against the budget the threat model already documents.

**The Kotlin bridge dropped a null pattern** instead of reporting it, so an
application that passed one narrowed its space to something it never wrote.
It now maps to the empty string, which is not a document name, so the core
refuses the call where it was made.

### Verification

Each fix is mutation-checked and fails only for its own mutation: dropping the
wipe clear, dropping either nudge guard, dropping the descriptor refusal, and
raising the app-side bound past the frame bound (which fails the build with
its own message). Each of the three code commits builds and passes on its own,
carrying one new test.

Green locally: `cargo fmt`, both clippy jobs, `cargo test --workspace` (1,831
in the engine crate, 0 failed), rustdoc under `-D warnings`,
`generate-bindings.sh` as a clean no-op, the Android JVM suite through the
standalone harness (the bridge change compiles), and the Python suite, 273
tests, against a freshly built cdylib.

prs.title: feat(protocol): remove a replicated document from every replica
prs.body:
Deleting a document removed it here and nowhere else. It was absent from this
device's next version offer and still present on the peer's, and the rules
that exist to carry a document a peer has never seen recreated and refilled
it. A delete was undone by the next exchange, with no error and no event. The
guide called that out as a gap, `wipeAll()` inherited it, and it is the first
of the three bullets under "What this version does not do".

## What this adds

`removeDoc(space, doc)` removes a document from every replica of its space,
and `removeSpace(space)` does it for every document a space holds. A replica
that applies one reports the new `data_doc_deleted` event with `by: "peer"`.

`deleteDoc` is unchanged, and is now documented as what it always was:
eviction. It drops this device's copy and records nothing about the name, so
a replica that still holds the document refills it. `wipeAll()` is unchanged
too, and records no removals, because a logout has to leave a custom backend
empty.

## The design, in three sentences

**A removal is a version, not a flag.** It records the version the document
stood at, and that version is the floor: content at or below it is what the
removal decided about, and anything beyond it is an edit made concurrently
with the removal or after it. Carrying the version rather than a bare "this
is gone" is what lets every replica reach the same answer without knowing
which happened first.

**An edit beats a removal**, and brings the whole document back rather than
the edit alone, because the edit was made on the old contents and its history
*is* those contents. There is no version of this rule that returns one
without the other, so the alternative was discarding the edit. It arrives as
an ordinary `data_changed` on a document the application removed, and the
docs say so.

**The floor is written before the records it removes.** The reverse order
leaves, after a crash in between, records whose presence votes the document
back into existence at the next open, which is the resurrection the whole
mechanism exists to prevent. A crash in the new order leaves a name every
reader already treats as removed, and the next open finishes the job.

## Compatibility

Negotiated as `data_versions` entry 4, appended. A peer without it ignores
the new field, keeps its copy, and offers it back on every exchange; the
removing side refuses each offer and each blob against its own record, so the
removal holds there regardless. Nothing loops and nothing is surfaced
wrongly.

An offer with no removals serialises byte-identically to what this release
sends today, which is why all eight frozen wire vectors still pass unchanged.

New sealed storage category `data_doc_meta`. No new error code, so the
append-only FFI enum is untouched. No config change.

## Two bugs found while building it

- A blob from beyond the floor was refused by `open_doc`, because the name
  still read as removed, so the edit-wins case could never complete. The name
  now comes back at the point where "beyond the floor" has just been
  established.
- The floor check in the catch-up loop was wrong in general: every version
  vector includes the empty one, so a replica that re-created a name and had
  nothing in it yet read as holding removed content, and the document it was
  waiting for was never sent. The check belongs only where the document is
  absent locally.

## Verification

Eleven mechanisms mutation-checked, each failing only for its own mutation.
One came back uncaught and was a genuine coverage gap rather than a redundant
guard: excluding removed names when a space loads only matters when records
*survive* a removal, which only a crash produces. That case now has a test
that seeds a dead record through the sealed writer and relaunches.

Green locally: `cargo fmt`, `clippy --workspace -D warnings`,
`clippy -p offline-protocol --no-default-features`, `cargo test --workspace`
(2,912 passed), `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, regenerated bindings,
the uniffi drift guards, the Android JVM suite, `tsc --noEmit`, and the
Python suite against a real cdylib.

## Docs

Every one of the eleven places that said there were no deletion tombstones
now says what is true: the spec chapter (new Deletion section), the
replication state machine, the capability chapter, the guide, the API
reference, UPGRADING, `configuration.md`, both bridge docs, the threat model,
the UDL, the React Native types, and two code comments.
